tip: умеет (umeet) means know how to, a learned skill, not passing ability. не умеет плавать (ne umeet plavat) = never learned to swim.
Russian gives age with the person in the dative, not the nominative. Ему (Emu = to him) is that dative, meaning he is the one who is twenty-five.
нравится (nravitsya = is pleasing) puts the liker in the dative. Мне (Mne = to me) is that dative, so the line reads the movie does not please me.
по (po) plus the dative marks a repeated occasion. по выходным (po vykhodnym) = on weekends, meaning every weekend, not a single one.
нет (net = there is no) forces the genitive on the missing thing. нет времени (net vremeni = no time) uses the genitive, not the nominative.
стоит (stoit = is worth) with a dative person gives soft advice. Тебе (Tebe = to you) не стоит (ne stoit) means you would be better off not doing it.
Seasons take the instrumental to mean in that season. осенью (osen'yu = in autumn) needs no preposition, the ending alone carries in.
пахнет (pakhnet = smells) takes the instrumental for the scent. свежей выпечкой (svezhey vypechkoy) = of fresh baking, with no separate word for of.
Numbers five and above take a genitive plural noun. пять учеников (pyat uchenikov = students) uses the genitive plural, not the plain plural.
могли бы (mogli by) is the polite could you. The particle бы (by) is what softens a request into would you mind.
меня зовут (menya zovut = me they call) is the standard way to give your name. меня (menya) is the object, so there is no word for I.
ни ... ни (ni ... ni = neither ... nor) still needs не on the verb. не знаем (ne znaem = we do not know) keeps the double negative English drops.
One sentence, two aspects. строили (stroili) shows the building in progress, построили (postroili) marks it finally completed.
ехал (ekhal = was riding) is the vehicle verb. Russian picks ехать (ekhat) for wheels and идти (idti) for on foot, a split English does not mark.
